'''Said Amin (Gabe)<ref name=ICTV_obit /> Ghabrial''' (October 1, 1939 – November 26, 2018<ref name=KB_obit>{{citation |url=http://www.kerrbrothersfuneralhome.com/obituaries.php?view=detail&id=13283 |title=Said A. Ghabrial |publisher=Kerr Brothers Funeral Home |access-date=30 May 2019 }}</ref>) was an [[List of Egyptian Americans|Egyptian-American]] [[plant pathology|plant pathologist]], known for his work on [[mycovirus]]es – viruses of fungi – and particularly their effects on the [[virulence]] of [[Plant pathology#Fungi|plant-pathogenic fungi]].<ref name=APS_bio /> He also researched [[bean pod mottle virus]], an economically important [[soybean]] disease. He was professor of plant pathology at the [[University of Kentucky]] (1986–2014).

==Early life and education==
Ghabrial was born in [[Cairo]], where he attended public schools and then the College of Agriculture at [[Cairo University]], gaining a BS in agriculture (1959).<ref name=ARV_auto>{{citation |title=My Life and Virus Research Journey |author=Said A. Ghabrial |journal=[[Annual Review of Virology]] |volume=5 |pages=1–32 |year=2018 |issue=1 |doi=10.1146/annurev-virology-092917-043507 |pmid=30265631 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=UKentucky_bio>{{citation |url=https://plantpathology.ca.uky.edu/person/said-ghabrial |title=Said Ghabrial  |publisher=Department of Plant Pathology, University of Kentucky |access-date=30 May 2019}}</ref> He worked at the Egyptian Ministry of Land Reform (1959–61) and then briefly did national service in the Egyptian Army.<ref name=ARV_auto /> In 1961, he went to the United States on a government scholarship, and studied in the Plant Pathology Department of [[Louisiana State University]], where he gained an MS (1963) and PhD (1965) in plant pathology,<ref name=ARV_auto /><ref name=UKentucky_bio /> supervised by Thomas Pirone. His MS research was on [[tomato leaf mold]], a fungal disease of tomatoes caused by ''Cladosporium fulvum'' (''[[Passalora fulva]]''). His PhD research was on wilting of [[Tabasco pepper]] (''[[Capsicum frutescens]]'') caused by [[tobacco etch virus]].<ref name=ARV_auto />

==Career and research==
Ghabrial carried out post-doctoral research at the [[University of California, Davis]], on [[Southern bean mosaic virus]] under Robert Shepherd and [[Raymond Grogan]] (1965–66). After returning to Egypt, where he worked for the Ministry of Agriculture on economically important plant viruses (1966–70), he moved to the United States and took up a post-doctoral position in the Botany and Plant Pathology Department of [[Purdue University]] (1970–72) under Richard M. Lister;<ref name=APS_bio>{{citation |url=https://www.apsnet.org/members/give-awards/awards/PastAwardees/Documents/2002awardees.pdf |title=Fellows: Said Amin Ghabrial |journal=[[Phytopathology (journal)|Phytopathology]] |volume=93 |page=20 |year=2003}}</ref><ref name=ARV_auto /> he worked on the segmented plant viruses [[tobacco rattle virus]] and [[tobacco streak virus]].<ref name=ARV_auto /> 

In 1972, Ghabrial moved to the [[University of Kentucky]], where he remained until his retirement, holding successively assistant (1972–75), associate (1975–86) and full professorships (1986–2014) in the Plant Pathology Department.<ref name=APS_bio /><ref name=ARV_auto /><ref name=UKentucky_bio /> He also held visiting professorships at the University of California, Davis (1978–79), [[Oregon State University]] (1988–89) and the [[University of California, Berkeley]] (2000–01).<ref name=ARV_auto /><ref name=UKentucky_bio /> 

One major focus of his research at Kentucky was on [[mycovirus]]es that infect [[Plant pathology#Fungi|fungal pathogens of plants]]. He discovered and characterized a virus in the ''[[Totiviridae]]'' family that infects the fungal pathogen ''[[Helminthosporium victoriae]]'', which causes the economically important disease Victoria blight in oats. Most fungal viruses do not affect their host but Ghabrial showed that the virus attenuates the [[virulence]] of the fungus.<ref name=APS_bio /><ref name=ARV_auto /><ref name=Ghabrial_AnnRevPhyto>{{citation |title=Viruses of plant pathogenic fungi |author=Said A. Ghabrial |author2=Nobuhiro Suzuki |journal=[[Annual Review of Phytopathology]] |volume=47 |pages=353–84 |year=2009 |issue=1 |doi=10.1146/annurev-phyto-080508-081932 |pmid=19400634|bibcode=2009AnRvP..47..353G }}</ref> This raises the possibility that such viruses might in future be used in the [[Biological pest control|biological control]] of plant diseases caused by fungi.<ref name=Ghabrial_AnnRevPhyto /> Another long-term research focus was viral diseases of [[soybean]] (''Glycine max''), particularly the economically important [[bean pod mottle virus]].<ref name=ARV_auto />

He was elected a fellow of the [[American Phytopathological Society]] in 2002.<ref name=APS_bio /><ref name=UKentucky_bio /> He twice chaired the [[International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses]]'s fungal virus subcommittee (1987–93 and 2011–14)<ref name=ICTV_obit>{{citation |url=https://talk.ictvonline.org/information/w/news/856/page |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200609113657/https://talk.ictvonline.org/information/w/news/856/page  |archive-date=June 9, 2020 |title=Remembering Said "Gabe" Ghabrial |publisher=[[International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses]] |date=November 27, 2018 |access-date=30 May 2019 }}</ref> and was one of the editors of the sixth edition (1995) of its ''Virus Taxonomy'' report. He authored or co-authored around 150 articles in peer-reviewed journals as well as many book chapters.<ref>{{citation |url=https://plantpathology.ca.uky.edu/content/ghabrial-publications|title=Ghabrial Publications |publisher=Department of Plant Pathology, University of Kentucky |access-date=30 May 2019}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Ghabrial married Karlin Upton Ghabrial, whom he met in Davis, in 1966. They had a son and two daughters.<ref name=ARV_auto /> He died on November 26, 2018.<ref name=KB_obit />
